title: Enclosure

definition.text: Enclosure was the English practice of fencing off 'waste' or common land and taking it over, which stripped commoners of their traditional rights to use it.

facts.text: It merged scattered strips of land into large fields bounded by hedges, walls or fences, kept for the sole use of individual owners or their tenants.
Enclosure happened by owners making 'closes', by groups of proprietors enclosing whole parishes, and by acts of Parliament, the first in 1604.
Its stated aim was more efficient farming, but enclosed land also became much more valuable.
In Tudor England high wool profits led lords to turn common arable land into sheep pasture, evicting villagers.
Historians see enclosure riots as the leading form of social protest from the 1530s to the 1640s.
The movement probably peaked from 1760 to 1832, and surplus rural labour moved to towns to become industrial workers.
The Hammonds said enclosure ruined small farmers, cottagers and squatters, while Chambers and Mingay argued it brought more food, more cultivated land and more rural jobs.
Many Marxists see enclosure as 'primitive accumulation' that laid the ground for capitalism.

contested_note: Historians disagree on whether enclosure mainly impoverished rural people or raised food output and rural employment.

definition.text: Before enclosure, English common land lay under the manorial lord, with a manor made up of peasant tenants' holdings and the lord's own demesne farm.

facts.text: Tenants held rights such as pasture, pannage and estovers, and landless peasants often farmed narrow 'waste' strips nobody officially used.
Its end came with new methods such as the Norfolk four-course rotation, which raised crop and livestock yields by improving soil fertility and cutting fallow periods.

definition.text: Community forestry is a participatory approach, prominent since the 1970s, in which local communities take an active part in managing forests and deciding land use.

facts.text: The FAO defines it as any situation that closely involves local people in forestry.
It manages forests both for income from timber and non-timber products and for ecosystem services such as watershed protection and carbon storage.
It is seen as one of the most promising ways to combine forest conservation with rural development and poverty reduction.
Nepal's democratically run Forest User Groups have regenerated forests, with some regions seeing a 37% rise in forest cover.
Secure land tenure decides whether communities can invest in sustainable practices; unclear boundaries, elite capture and weak enforcement threaten projects.
Certification and carbon credits open global markets, but high certification costs remain a barrier for smallholders.
There is no single blueprint, because regional social, economic and environmental conditions differ.

definition.text: The IAD framework is Elinor Ostrom's theoretical tool for studying how people, called actors, interact with common-pool resources.

facts.text: Common-pool resources are rivalrous, since one person's use reduces others', and non-excludable, since keeping people out is impractical; forests and pastures are examples.
Built on rational choice assumptions, it explains outcomes by documenting governance structures, actors' positions and formal and informal rules.
It breaks complex collective action problems into smaller 'action arenas'.
Institutions are studied through seven rule types: position, boundary, choice, aggregation, information, pay-off and scope.

title: International Association for the Study of the Commons
article: International Association for the Study of the Commons

definition.text: A non-profit association founded in 1989 to advance understanding of institutions for managing resources held or used in common.

facts.text: It publishes the open-access International Journal of the Commons and holds biennial global conferences.
Elinor Ostrom was a founding member and its first president.
